ELPD Releases Footage of Controversial August Arrest Outside Harper’s
articles.description: Watch the footage from the controversial Aug. 2 arrest.
articles.content: Long-awaited police body camera footage of an East Lansing police officer punching a 20-year-old woman while she was being detained at the beginning of August was released by the city Tuesday. In addition to multiple police body camera recordings, the package of videos includes footage taken from the patio at Harper’s Restaurant and Brew Pub, across the street and within the jail. The 12 videos released by the city can be viewed here. Footage from the patio and from a parking lot across the street shows the woman, Myana Collins, climb the fencing on Harper’s patio after standing and sitting near the line in front of the bar’s entrance. From there Collins approaches the entrance but is stopped outside by individuals alongside security. Police body camera footage and other footage from the entrance shows that an officer tells Collins, who is sitting on the patio, that business staff has asked her to leave the premises. Body camera footage from the officer speaking to her shows Collins say she’s waiting for her friends. The officer informs her that if she continues to sit on the patio, she will go to jail for trespassing. Collins is seen in the body camera footage walking around the patio before attempting to go through the Harper’s entrance. The officer is seen grabbing Collins’ purse strap, pulling her away from the door and instructing her to go down the stairs before a struggle ensues, with Collins ending up on the ground. An officer is heard in the body camera footage telling Collins to put her hands behind her back as she says the officer is “being rude” to her. Still on the ground, an officer informs Collins that she will be tased, prior to deploying a taser. Officers say throughout the various videos that the taser shot three probes into her leg and one in her arm and the probes “bounced out” after hitting her. After officers carry Collins down the stairs, body camera footage shows an officer telling Collins, who has her arms handcuffed behind her back as she’s laying face down on the ground, to stop grabbing and assaulting officers. This is when one of the officers punches Collins in the arm while she’s on the ground with a closed fist three times. During this interaction Collins is screaming for help, saying she can’t breathe and that the officers are being racist. Back in August, a concerned bystander published a video of the incident, showing an East Lansing police officer punching Collins multiple times. The footage, taken near the bottom of the front steps of Harper’s, sparked immediate outrage from members of the East Lansing community who questioned the actions of the officers involved. The city’s initial response asserted that the video did not paint a full picture of the incident, with a news release published by the city on Aug. 3 saying the city would review footage of the interaction to determine what can be shared with the public. It’s been about three months since this interaction occurred and the city has maintained that the officers involved acted in a professional manner. After the Ingham County Prosecutor’s Office declined to authorize felony charges against Collins in September, East Lansing Police Chief Jennifer Brown said the city attorney’s office would review the incident to consider charges. Earlier this month, city attorneys announced they would not be pursuing charges against Collins. “After a careful review of this case and the information that has come to light in recent weeks, we have decided not to pursue charges in this case,” East Lansing City Attorney Carlito Young said in an Oct. 16 press release. “However, I want to make it clear that this decision does not call into question the propriety of the officers’ decisions on the night of Ms. Collins’ arrest. They responded to a difficult and rapidly evolving situation, cooperated fully with all subsequent reviews and have maintained professionalism throughout more than two months of public scrutiny.” Members of the City Council say residents can form opinions based on footage, as NAACP Lansing branch president says video shows “torture.” The cell phone footage posted of Collins’ arrest in August sparked broad backlash against the ELPD during public meetings, but the controversy did not happen in a vacuum. Questions about police use of force in a series of incidents, including the April 15 fatal shooting of Isaiah Kirby, have raised concerns about the police department. In September, a report prepared by Adrian College Criminal Justice and Sociology Professor Cedrick Heraux for the city’s Police Oversight Commission showed a surge in ELPD use of force in 2025 and that Black people were much more likely to be subjected to severe force than white people. A community group has formed to watch police interactions with residents downtown during weekends. Local advocates and the Lansing NAACP branch have called for the resignation or removal of Chief Brown. After the city released the footage of Collins’ arrest, East Lansing Info called the five members of the City Council on Wednesday to ask for their thoughts on what the footage shows. Councilmember Mark Meadows and Mayor Erik Altmann each declined to share an opinion on the videos, but encouraged residents to review the footage and draw their own conclusions. Meadows said he would have liked footage to be released earlier, but the city was following its attorneys’ advice to wait for a decision on whether or not to charge Collins with a crime. “People show up at the microphone [during City Council meetings] and even at the last meeting, a couple of them said ‘we’re just speculating,’” Meadows said. “Well, this helps us not speculate.” Earlier in October, the council endorsed new police use of force policies after some council members said they think the body should take a more active role in addressing concerns about policing. Altmann said he is not aware of any other actions on the horizon the council could take that impact policing. Councilmember Steve Whelan said he is not a spokesperson for the police department and does not make decisions on discipline. However, he did comment on the footage. Whelan, who worked for the ELPD for 25 years before retiring last year, said the officer told Collins to stop grabbing him several times before he deployed “distractionary strikes” to get her to comply with commands. Whelan said it is painful for officers to have their legs grabbed or pinched. “I did hear the officer say five times that he was being hurt and that does make a difference to me,” Whelan said. “That hurt needs to stop.” Mayor Pro Tem Chuck Grigsby said he had nothing to add beyond comments he has already made at public meetings and Councilmember Kerry Ebersole Singh did not respond to a voicemail left at about noon on Wednesday. NAACP Lansing Branch President James McCurtis Jr. said he believed the interaction was appalling based on the cell phone footage he saw previously and the newly released videos do not change that belief. He said Collins was not treated humanely and questioned if officers would have been so forceful with a young, blonde, white woman, referencing Heraux’s report and other reports showing a history of racial disparities in East Lansing policing. “There is no reason why she should have been punched three times after being handcuffed and placed face down on concrete, and not just face down, but legs up, in a sense almost hogtied,” McCurtis said. “To me it was torture.” It is common for police in East Lansing to deal with young people who are intoxicated, McCurtis said, and there were several police officers on scene to deal with one woman. “Do we see other kids getting beaten in that way?” McCurtis asked. Brown needs to be fired so the culture within the ELPD can begin to change, McCurtis said. He also said all five members of the City Council should be voted out when their terms are up. “This is the only police department in this area where we see this type of activity,” McCurtis said. “Where we see this type of excessive force on a continual basis. It’s one event after another.” Do you have a question that you would like ELi to investigate? Just click here! articles.title: US warns allies to prepare for possible Iran strikes, retaliation after elections, AP sources say
articles.description: US warns allies to prepare for possible Iran strikes, retaliation after elections, AP sources say AP News U.S. Warns Gulf of Possible Short, Intense Renewal of Iran War After Midterms WSJ Military choices for Iran are being readied for president as midterm elections loom: officials Fox News Trump says Iran war will end 'when I want it to' as costs reportedly balloon to $47 billion CNBC Trump weighs post-midterms Iran
articles.content: WASHINGTON (AP) — U.S. officials have told several Middle East countries and regional allies to be prepared for potential renewed military action against Iran after next week’s midterm elections in the United States — as well as the possibility that Iran will attempt to retaliate against them, according to two diplomats briefed on the matter. Both of the diplomats spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to comment about the sensitive warnings conveyed by U.S. diplomats and defense officials. President Donald Trump has not made a final decision on whether to carry out new strikes against Iran, the diplomats stressed. The president, however, has repeatedly said that he is weighing ordering new military action once the critical Nov. 3 elections in the United States are over. Those threats and the fresh U.S. urgings for allies to prepare for potential retaliation are putting the region on alert that a return to major operations could now be on the horizon. The U.S. is warning Middle East allies that attacks against Iran may resume soon. AP correspondent Jennifer King reports. The White House and U.S. officials declined to comment. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Wednesday in a post on X that Tehran “continues to give diplomacy a chance to succeed” and is working with mediators to review ideas that Tehran included in a proposal floated last month — summarily rejected by Trump — that the Iranians still want to see used as the basis to return to a ceasefire. Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates foreign ministry issued a statement urging the sides to “exercise wisdom and pursue political solutions to help contain tensions” and prevent a return to full-scale operations in the war that began in late February. The U.S. has told regional allies that the new round of military action could last for several days, but regional officials are bracing for Iran and its proxy groups to retaliate — leading to a fight that could last even longer, the diplomats said. The allies have also been urged by U.S. officials to take precautionary measures in anticipation that Iran’s response will include retaliatory strikes on energy facilities and other crucial infrastructure. While the U.S. has not carried out a strike against Iran since early September, the situation in the Middle East has become more complicated. The conflict has spread, with Iran-backed Houthi rebels carrying out attacks on Saudi Arabia’s oil infrastructure and airports. A Saudi-led coalition has responded with its own deadly attacks on Houthi-held territory in Yemen. The Wall Street Journal reported earlier on Gulf nations being briefed to be prepared for potential escalation by the U.S. It’s unclear how soon after Election Day that the U.S. military would be ready to potentially resume strikes. The Pentagon late last month deployed the USS Theodore Roosevelt, along with a series of amphibious landing ships with Marines aboard -- roughly 9,000 troops in all -- from San Diego to the Persian Gulf to bolster the U.S. military in the region. At the time, one U.S. official said this deployment could lead to an unusually high naval presence of more than 20,000 sailors and Marines, as well as hundreds of aircraft, in the region, which has only occurred a handful of times in the last two decades. The Navy had three carrier strike groups in the Middle East in April for the first time since 2003. Late Wednesday, reports emerged that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had fired the Pentagon’s top military planner. Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia was removed as head of strategy, plans and policy on the Joint Chiefs of Staff, according to a defense official who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive personnel matters. That official said there is no immediate replacement for Sylvia and no reason has been given for the firing. Trump, who has focused in recent weeks on campaigning for Republicans ahead of the Nov. 3 elections, has been evasive about what he plans to do next with Iran. The war has proved to be a heavy weight on Republican candidates as they make their case to voters who are fatigued by rising gasoline prices, a byproduct of the war that’s driven up costs across nearly every sector in the global economy. The cost of fighting the Iran war to American taxpayers has grown to $47.1 billion, according to the latest estimate the Pentagon has provided to Congress. While campaigning for Republicans, Trump has consistently assured voters that the war’s end is near, while also threatening that a new round of bombing could be coming once the election passes. During a campaign stop in Lubbock, Texas, on Tuesday, Trump said a conclusive end to the eight-month-old conflict could be coming “in a couple of weeks, if you don’t mind.” “Somebody asked me before, when will the war in Iran end?” Trump said earlier in the same address. “I said, ‘Whenever I want it to end.’ It’ll be very quick, but we have to have it end properly, with total and complete -- a total statement, they will never have a nuclear weapon.” Trump may be looking at a postelection timeline for possible action, but the region is on edge that Tehran could do something provocative before then -- especially if they feel U.S. actions is imminent, said Jonathan Schanzer, executive director at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a hawkish Washington think tank. “Why would they wait until after the elections here ... if they could initiate it and potentially gain the upper hand?” he said. Magdy reported from New York. AP writers Konstantin Toropin and Seung Min Kim contributed reporting.

Justice Department makes a splash with politically sensitive cases and actions during midterm blitz
articles.description: Justice Department makes a splash with politically sensitive cases and actions during midterm blitz AP News Comey, Hutchinson and more Trump foes are in Justice Dept.’s pre-election sights The Washington Post DOJ’s ‘shocking’ flurry of pre-election activity breaks long-standing precedent, former officials say NBC News Trump's Department of Justice is wading into elections in unprecedented ways NPR Justice Department
articles.content: WASHINGTON (AP) — A crucial and contentious midterm election arrives next week, and President Donald Trump’s Justice Department has been scrambling with a blitz of headline-making actions and cases that defense lawyers, Democrats and other critics say is no coincidence and reeks of politics — in both the timing and the targets. This month alone, the Justice Department escalated an investigation into Democratic U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar with a search of her home; brought criminal charges against two former FBI officials accused of falsely downplaying their knowledge of investigations involving Hunter Biden; revealed a fresh attempt to prosecute former FBI Director James Comey; and made an unsuccessful attempt to indict a former White House aide who delivered dramatic but disputed testimony about Trump’s efforts to overturn the 2020 election. That’s on top of lawsuits in Alaska and California related to next week’s voting. The moves are notable not only because of the timing but also because they largely have been directed at outspoken critics of Trump or issues that have animated the Republican’s base. The Justice Department has also employed unusual maneuvers to lock down charges, bypassing grand juries to file what are effectively placeholder cases against Comey and the ex-FBI officials in the heavily Democratic nation’s capital — where prosecutors over the past year have repeatedly struggled to secure indictments. “Never in the modern history of the Department of Justice has there ever been such a brazen disregard for time-honored norms and protocols in conceiving of or undertaking politically sensitive investigations,” said David Laufman, who served as a senior Justice Department official across Democratic and Republican administrations and helped oversee the Hillary Clinton email investigation. The Justice Department, in a statement, said it is “following the facts and the law, not anyone’s political timetable.” The law enforcement agency has a long-accepted practice of avoiding overt investigative actions against candidates in the weeks before an election, or other public steps that could be perceived as attempting to influence a political outcome. It’s such a foundational principle that successive attorneys general have issued departmentwide memos during election cycles reminding employees not to make an investigative move designed to help or hinder any particular candidate. Responding to questions about the recent investigative moves, the Justice Department said in a statement that it was an informal practice, not a written rule, to avoid overt actions within 60 days of an election. The practice is meant to prohibit prosecutors from choosing the timing of an action to affect an election, the department said. “The standard is purpose, not proximity to Election Day. Department policy does not require the Department to stop ongoing work during an election season,” the department said. That practice was famously tested in 2016 when Comey, then the FBI director, told Congress 11 days before Election Day that the bureau was revisiting its investigation into Democratic nominee Hillary Clinton’s handling of classified information because of newly discovered emails. Comey has said he felt he picked the least destructive option available, but his decision-making was harshly criticized by Democrats — and the Justice Department inspector general. Attorney General Todd Blanche, for his part, has not been shy about his view that the Justice Department does not exist independent of the White House and has insisted he is no different from his predecessors in serving a president. He has denied that the department’s investigative decisions are political. Yet even before this month, the Justice Department had initiated multiple inquiries into the president’s perceived adversaries. That includes a Florida-based investigation that Trump allies had hoped would prove a right-wing theory that former law enforcement and intelligence officials who scrutinized the president over the last decade had conspired against him. That investigation has shown signs of faltering amid a spate of staff turnovers and delays. Investigators in recent weeks have put off scheduled grand jury testimony of multiple witnesses, according to multiple people familiar with the matter who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss an ongoing investigation. Among the most politically delicate moves this month came when federal agents searched the home of Omar, one of the most outspoken congressional critics of the president. She is on the ballot Tuesday for another term representing Minnesota’s 5th District. Federal agents seized Omar’s phone in the search and have issued more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas, including to some of her relatives, as investigators probe issues related to her immigration paperwork. Blanche has defended the timing of the search, which was approved by a federal judge. He told reporters last week, “I can tell you unequivocally that the decision to seek a search warrant had nothing to do with what’s happening in November.” The Justice Department later charged two former FBI officials with making false statements to Congress about their knowledge of a laptop the department says belonged to former President Joe Biden’s son Hunter. The case emerged from an investigation that began immediately after a July speech on election security by Trump and was ordered by FBI Director Kash Patel, according to testimony Tuesday from an FBI agent assigned to the probe. The Justice Department charged the two former officials by complaint instead of a grand jury indictment — a move the magistrate judge overseeing the case described as unusual. Prosecutors then left the judge dumbfounded when they tried to add another charge by filing a new criminal complaint on the court docket without the required judicial sign-off that probable cause exists. “Everything is a little sideshow on top of a sideshow,” U.S. Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui told prosecutors. On Monday, newly unsealed court papers in a separate case revealed that prosecutors are attempting to bring the third criminal case against Comey since Trump returned to the White House, accusing him of leaking classified information a decade ago. With the statute of limitations set to expire earlier this month, prosecutors used an uncommon legal tactic in an attempt to extend the time in which they can seek a grand jury indictment. Comey’s legal team has described it as legally invalid and politically motivated, and is pushing the judge to dismiss it. A judge is set to hear arguments Friday. Asked about the latest case against the former FBI director, Trump said this week that he didn’t know anything about it. But the president added, “He’s a dirty cop, James Comey.” For his part, Comey seemed unsurprised. “Well, they’re back — again,” he said in a video statement Monday. “It would almost be funny if it weren’t such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice — one that we cannot become numb to. Nothing’s changed with me; I’m still innocent, I’m still not afraid of these people — and I still believe in the independent federal judiciary.”

Microsoft recorded $10 billion in revenue from OpenAI
articles.description: Microsoft said it made $10 billion in revenue from commercial arrangements with OpenAI, including revenue-sharing payments, in the quarter ending September 30. It underscores the still-enormous financial dependency of the partnership.
articles.content: Microsoft generated $10 billion in revenue from commercial arrangements with OpenAI, including revenue-sharing payments, in the quarter ended September 30, the company said in a regulatory filing on Wednesday. That represents nearly 11% of Microsoft’s total quarterly revenue of $92.3 billion, highlighting the enormous financial ties that remain between the two companies even as they increasingly compete for the same customers. (Microsoft’s financial year begins in July, making the quarter ended September 30, 2026 the first quarter of its fiscal 2027.) For the full 2026 fiscal year, revenue from OpenAI hit $24.1 billion. At its latest quarterly pace, Microsoft would pull in $40 billion annually from OpenAI-related arrangements. Microsoft also reported $7.2 billion in outstanding receivables from OpenAI at the end of September, up from $6 billion at the end of June. That money represents amounts OpenAI owes for previous transactions, not additional revenue. It’s not clear how much of Microsoft’s revenue from OpenAI came from revenue-sharing payments or Azure cloud computing services. TechCrunch has reached out for more information. In November 2025, TechCrunch reported, citing leaked documents, that Microsoft had received $865.8 million in net revenue-sharing payments from OpenAI during the first nine months of that year. OpenAI reportedly shares 20% of its revenue with Microsoft as part of a previous deal in which the software giant invested more than $13 billion in the AI startup. (Neither the AI lab nor Microsoft have publicly confirmed this percentage.) As part of an April 2026 agreement, OpenAI is on the hook to continue sharing revenue with Microsoft through 2030, subject to a cap, even as OpenAI is allowed to work with competing cloud providers. The companies began loosening the ties of their once-exclusive partnership in October 2025, when Microsoft relinquished its hold on OpenAI to give the startup more freedom to partner with other cloud providers. In exchange, OpenAI committed to buying an additional $250 billion in Azure services as part of an October 2025 agreement. Microsoft’s ownership stake in OpenAI has also declined slightly from about 25% in June to 24% in September. That continues a gradual decline from roughly 27% following the October 2025 recapitalization. Microsoft did not specify what caused the dilution. articles.title: Microsoft reveals strong cloud growth amid financial reporting overhaul
articles.description: Microsoft just posted the first quarter of its 2027 fiscal financial results. The software maker made $92.3 billion in revenue and a net income of $33.6 billion during Q1. Revenue is up 19 percent, and net income has increased by 32 percent. It's a new financial year for Microsoft, so the company is changing up how it reports its finances by splitting its businesses into two segments for the first time. Gone are the
articles.content: Microsoft just posted the first quarter of its 2027 fiscal financial results. The software maker made $92.3 billion in revenue and a net income of $33.6 billion during Q1. Revenue is up 19 percent, and net income has increased by 32 percent. It’s a new financial year for Microsoft, so the company is changing up how it reports its finances by splitting its businesses into two segments for the first time. Gone are the previous segments: Productivity and Business Processes, Intelligent Cloud, and More Personal Computing. It’s now just Agents and Infra, and Devices and Consumer. Agents and Infra, which includes businesses like Azure, Microsoft 365 commercial and consumer, and server products, makes up 83 percent ($76.8 billion) of the overall $92.3 billion of Microsoft’s revenue and has increased 25 percent year-over-year. The big changes to Microsoft’s financial reporting also mean we will now see the company disclose Azure revenue on a quarterly basis. Azure contributed $33.17 billion in revenue this quarter, up 48 percent year-over-year. Devices and Consumer, which includes Windows, Xbox, Surface, and Microsoft’s search and advertising businesses, makes up the remaining 17 percent ($15.5 billion) of Microsoft’s $92.3 billion in revenues this quarter — a decrease of three percent. [Image: Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra arrived on shelves earlier this month. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/VERGE_10_04_2026_0184.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Windows OEM and devices revenue is down 22 percent year-over-year, amid a RAMageddon crisis that has seen the overall PC market dropped by 20 percent in the recent quarter. Microsoft blames the revenue drop on the benefit of Windows 10 end of support during the prior year, as well as OEM inventory drawdowns and a weaker PC market. Microsoft launched Intel- and Qualcomm-powered Surface Pro 12 and Surface Laptop 8 devices just before its new financial year began, and the company even refreshed its smaller Surface Pro and Surface Laptop with Qualcomm’s X2 Plus chips during the quarter. Surface prices are higher than ever thanks to RAMageddon, and the PC market looks like it’s going to go through a very tough time during Microsoft’s 2027 financial year and beyond. Microsoft CFO Amy Hood said on the company’s earnings call that she expects Windows OEM revenue to decline again next quarter, around “the mid 30s,” and a decline is expected to continue throughout the 2027 financial year. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella also remarked on the company’s new hybrid AI push for Windows during the earnings call. “We are executing on our vision to bring hybrid intelligence to every desk in every home, making every PC a secure agent box,” said Nadella. “As more capable models run locally, we see an opportunity to make more intelligence effectively unmetered.” Microsoft and Nvidia unveiled a range of RTX Spark laptops earlier this month, including the Surface Laptop Ultra. The laptops ship with up to 128GB of unified memory, and are capable of running recent frontier models locally. [Image: The Xbox Series X25 console will mark 25 years of Xbox next month. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/06/XBOX-Series-X25-Limited-Edition_2-1bfdd2858ad74a2180ff-1900x1080-1.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Over on the Xbox side, hardware revenue has declined once again year-over-year. Xbox hardware revenue is down 14 percent. Xbox content and services, which includes Game Pass, is down 2 percent, too. Microsoft is still not giving an update on Game Pass subscriber numbers, after the company last reported it had 34 million subscribers more than two years ago. Overall Xbox revenue is down 2 percent. The first quarter of the 2027 financial year for Xbox has been dominated by a “reset” with thousands of layoffs and studios spun off. The layoffs aren’t over yet, with rumors more could arrive in November and January. In a memo earlier this year, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma said “we will return Xbox to player and revenue growth” by the end of fiscal year 2027 (which runs through next June). The aim, as Sharma puts it, is to “scale what works” so that by fiscal year 2030 Xbox is “halfway to our long-term daily-player goal with sustained double-digit growth in players and engagement and industry leading margins.” Sharma posted on X that Xbox was “making progress, with a lot more work ahead.” Sharma also revealed that PC platform revenue has grown in double digits this quarter, and that “console sales remain constrained by supply, with more demand than consoles available.” [Media: https://twitter.com/asha_shar/status/2115574497621463499] Hood says Xbox hardware revenue will decline again next quarter, but Xbox content and services revenue is expected to increase in the “mid to high single digits.” Sharma says Microsoft is “working to get more consoles into players’ hands, including through our expanded refurbishment program.” Microsoft’s cloud revenues were really the star of the earnings show again this quarter, a phrase I seem to always write every few months. Microsoft Cloud revenue contributed $63.9 billion towards Microsoft’s revenues this quarter, almost 70 percent. That’s up 30 percent year-over-year, thanks to strong demand for Azure and Microsoft 365 commercial cloud. Microsoft 365 commercial cloud revenue itself also grew 18 percent, thanks to higher revenue per user and upselling of premium options like Microsoft 365 Copilot, E5, and E7. Microsoft 365 consumer cloud revenue has also grown by 17 percent, driven by growth in revenue per user and subscriber growth of 7 percent. Nadella also discussed his vision for Microsoft’s own AI models on the company’s earnings call. “We also continue to make rapid progress with our first-party models,” said Nadella. “Our goal is to advance the cost to outcome frontier, which means delivering capabilities comparable to leading models within three to six months of their release at a fraction of the training cost, thereby allowing us to transfer those cost benefits to customers.” Update, October 28th: Article updated with comments from Microsoft CFO Amy Hood, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, and Xbox CEO Asha Sharma.

articles.title: The Metro: Oakland and Wayne County museum funding proposal leaves out Macomb
articles.description: Art and culture institutions in Macomb County typically receive a fraction of the grant funding Oakland and Wayne do, according to a study by a local non-profit. The post The Metro: Oakland and Wayne County museum funding proposal leaves out Macomb appeared first on WDET 101.9 FM.
articles.content: Art and culture institutions in Macomb County typically receive a fraction of the grant funding Oakland and Wayne do, according to a study by a local non-profit. Anton Art Center in Mount Clemens, Mich. This election, voters in Oakland and Wayne County are deciding on the “Southeast Michigan Public Historical Museum Authority Millage Proposal.” It’s a 10-year, $0.2 million property tax proposal that would guarantee funding through 2035 for the Charles H. Wright Museum of African American History, the Detroit Historical Museum and the Dossin Great Lakes Museum. Beyond that, there’s also a 15% allotment for other historical museums throughout Wayne and Oakland County. Missing from that proposal is Macomb County. That ties into a running narrative of Macomb not receiving the same level of funding for culture and the arts that its neighbors in Oakland and Wayne do. While budget numbers do vary from-year-to-year, a study by a Macomb nonprofit found that the county received about $36 in grant funding per-resident, while Oakland and Wayne Counties receive over $200 dollars. That means art and historical institutions in Macomb County face different fiscal realities compared to its neighbors. Matt Matthews is the executive director of the Anton Art Center in Mount Clemens. He stopped by The Metro to talk with Alex McLenon about arts and culture funding in Macomb County. articles.title: Iran war’s cost to American taxpayers grows to an estimated $47.1 billion
articles.description: Iran war’s cost to American taxpayers grows to an estimated $47.1 billion AP News Pentagon says Iran war has cost US taxpayers $47bn: What that means Al Jazeera Iran live updates: US military estimates war with Iran now costs $47.1 billion ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos The Trump admin said energy costs were a small price to pay in Iran war, but U.S. consumers are paying nearly 8x more than anyone e
articles.content: WASHINGTON (AP) — The cost of the Iran war to American taxpayers has grown to $47.1 billion, according to a new estimate the Pentagon has provided to Congress. The fallout from the conflict has become a key issue in the midterm elections and could increase as President Donald Trump leaves open the possibility of renewed hostilities. The figure from U.S. Central Command, which oversees operations in the Middle East, is as of Oct. 16 and offers the most up-to-date cost for the conflict since it was launched in late February by the United States and Israel. The latest price tag, obtained by The Associated Press this week, shows a $3.5 billion bump in U.S. spending since early September, when that figure stood at about $43.6 billion. The growing cost of the unpopular war and its economic ripple effects on energy prices could hurt Republicans in next week’s midterm elections. Voters on Tuesday will decide which political party controls Congress during Trump’s last two years in office. The Republican president has said new strikes on Iran are an option after the midterms and is sending more military resources to the Middle East, despite initially promising Americans a military campaign that would last only a matter of weeks. As the war’s costs in lives, tax dollars and economic impact grow, most voters say they want Congress to prioritize ending the conflict, according to a recent AP-NORC poll. The expense of the conflict and military spending in general are already a contentious issue on Capitol Hill, where the Trump administration is pushing for the passage of a historic $1.5 trillion military budget proposal. The White House also is asking lawmakers to approve a $95 billion package that would help fund the Iran war and other priorities. Wednesday marks eight months of the war, which Democrats have been trying to end through legislation that has failed to pass the Republican-controlled Congress. “Trump and his ego led us into this war with no plan, no authority, and no exit strategy,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York said in a news release. “Senate Democrats will continue to do everything in our power to end this disaster of a war and stop the costs, chaos, and corruption seeping from the White House.” In the latest estimate, the bulk of the war’s costs are for replacing munitions, at about $29 billion. The advanced weapons most in demand and whose stockpiles have been drawn down are defensive missile interceptors, such as those launched by the Army’s Patriot and THAAD systems, with a single Patriot interceptor costing millions of dollars. The Pentagon says about $11.9 billion is related to costs of operations, while an additional $6 billion is tied to equipment losses. The Air Force’s costs are now $7.6 billion, and the Army’s are more than $2 billion. The Navy’s costs were listed at $1.45 billion, which is a significant drop from the $2.2 billion listed in early September. When asked why the Navy’s cost estimates decreased over the roughly six-week period, both the Navy and U.S. Central Command referred the questions to the Pentagon, which did not immediately respond to emails requesting comment on the new cost estimates. An Iranian missile is displayed under the country’s national flag in a military exhibition commemorating the anniversary of the start of the 1980-88 Iraq-Iran war at Baharestan Square, in Tehran, Monday, Sept. 28, 2026. (AP Photo/Vahid Salemi) An Iranian missile is displayed under the country’s national flag in a military exhibition commemorating the anniversary of the start of the 1980-88 Iraq-Iran war at Baharestan Square, in Tehran, Monday, Sept. 28, 2026. (AP Photo/Vahid Salemi) The latest estimate does not include damage to U.S. bases in the Middle East, which the Islamic Republic has attacked with ballistic missiles and drones. A report from the Pentagon inspector general released last month said Iranian strikes have damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and other structures at U.S. bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan. The Pentagon’s official tally lists 21 service members killed and 865 wounded in the conflict. That count includes troops who died in medical events and other situations that do not have a direct connection to the conflict, with 18 service members having been killed from Iranian strikes, combat aircraft crashes or disposal of Iranian drones. While Trump has mused repeatedly about whether to make a deal with Iran or “finish them off,” a third aircraft carrier and thousands of additional troops are making their way to the region. The Trump administration also has reduced staffing at some U.S. Embassies after receiving intelligence that Iran has stepped up efforts to target American personnel. Follow the AP’s coverage of the Iran war at https://apnews.com/hub/iran.

articles.title: Center Line Public school administrator named state’s Middle School Principal of the Year
articles.content: A veteran educator with 26 years of experience in Center Line Public Schools, including 10 years in administration, has been selected as Michigan’s 2027 High School Assistant Principal of the Year. John Grob, assistant principal of Center Line High School, was recently named by the Michigan Association of Secondary School Principals as the top assistant principal in the state. Grob joined the school district as an administrator in 2021 and brought an “innovative and data-focused mindset” to teaching and learning, school and MASSP officials said. Superintendent Joe Haynes said Grob’s “superpower is his ability to interact with people. Students know him as someone who holds them to high standards while never letting them forget they are cared for; staff know him as a steady partner, a generous mentor and the first to offer help — and the last to take credit.” Grob was surprised with the award by MASSP Executive Director Colin Ripmaster during a school-wide assembly attended by students, teachers and Center Line Public Schools leadership. In nominating Grob for the honor, Center Line High School Assistant Principal Mandolyn Grattan said he guided her in her first year as an assistant principal by asking questions, exploring different perspectives and helping her build confidence in her own decisions. “John has helped our staff see how they fit together as part of a larger instructional vision,” she said. MASSP officials said Grob’s Data Den initiative brings departments together to connect core standards, learning intentions and student data, helping teachers align their practices with shared instructional goals. Grob supports new teachers, mentors fellow administrators and helps colleagues work through challenges independent, Center Line school leaders said. He also introduced regular, non-evaluative classroom walkthroughs that help educators identify effective practices, examine student learning and refine instruction, according to staff members. He brings his observations full circle through professional learning, classroom modeling and practical applications of artificial intelligence to help teachers unpack standards and design lessons, they said. Grattan said Grob’s greatest gift as an administrator is “he makes the people around him better. He is generous with his time, ideas and expertise.” Grob will represent Michigan as its nominee for the National Principals Association High School Assistant Principal of the Year competition. All state award winners will be recognized at the National Education Leadership Awards ceremony in February 2027 in Tampa, Fla. This marked the second time in one week that MASSP officials were in Macomb County. Last week, Brad Martz, principal of Romeo Middle School, was named as the top middle school leader in the state.
